opus-5.5.text:
I think the natural intuition people have is that you should wait until AI is clearly generating a lot of value, and then scale up the investment in response. But I think that gets the timing roughly backwards, or at least it's too conservative.

The returns to AI depend heavily on the scale of compute you train and deploy with. If you look at the history of the field, capabilities have improved fairly predictably as you scale up training compute, and a lot of the economically interesting capabilities seem to arrive only past certain thresholds. So the value you get later is downstream of investments you make earlier. Fabs take years to build. Data centers and power infrastructure take years. If you wait until the revenue is obviously there, you've effectively delayed the arrival of that value by the length of the construction cycle.

So my view is that it's rational for investment to run somewhat ahead of realized revenue, in the same way it did for railways, electrification, or telecom. You build the infrastructure in anticipation of demand, because the expected payoff, if these systems can substitute for a large share of human labor, is enormous. We're talking about a potential prize on the order of tens of trillions of dollars a year in labor compensation globally. Against that, even hundreds of billions per year of capex can look modest, provided you put meaningful probability on reaching that kind of capability.

That doesn't mean there's no risk of overbuilding. You could have periods where capacity outruns what the models can actually do, and some investors will lose money, as happened in the dot-com era with fiber. But the fact that some bets fail doesn't make the overall strategy irrational. I'd frame it as: the optimal path probably involves investment scaling up before the economic value is fully visible, with a willingness to absorb some volatility along the way. Being too cautious has costs too. They're just less visible, because they show up as value that arrives later than it could have.

r002.rationale: It says building infrastructure early avoids delaying value because construction takes years, but does not say this reduces the adjustment costs of expanding abruptly when needed.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify early large AI training runs as a way to learn how to expand compute infrastructure.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it has to lead the value, and that's what makes this period so uncomfortable. Chips and data centers have very long lead times. A fab takes years to build, a large data center campus takes a couple of years from permitting to power to racks actually running, and the power infrastructure behind that can take even longer. So if you believe AI is going to be generating very large amounts of economic value within, say, a decade, you can't wait for that value to show up on the income statement and then start building. By the time the demand is visible, you're already three or four years behind.

So the investment has to be made on expectations rather than on realized revenue. And that's true of basically every major infrastructure build-out historically. Railways, electrification, telecom in the late nineties, these were all built ahead of demand, and some of them were overbuilt. The question is whether the overbuilding is catastrophic or just a bit wasteful.

My view is that the current scale of investment, which is maybe a few hundred billion dollars a year in compute infrastructure, is actually fairly small relative to the plausible value. If AI systems get to the point where they can substitute for a meaningful fraction of cognitive labor, you're talking about something that touches tens of trillions of dollars of global wages. Against that backdrop, spending a few percent of that annually on the capital stock that makes it possible looks reasonable, maybe even conservative. The risk is more on the timing than on the magnitude. If the capabilities arrive a few years later than investors expect, you get a lot of stranded capital, and that can create a bust that slows things down.

What I'd want to see is investment that scales with the evidence. Right now we have strong evidence that scaling compute continues to produce capability gains, and we're starting to see real revenue, in the tens of billions, from AI products. That's enough to justify a big build-out, but you'd want investors to be updating continuously rather than committing to a fixed trajectory regardless of what the models actually do. The worst outcome is a boom-bust cycle that leaves infrastructure half-built. The best outcome is that compute capacity grows roughly in step with demonstrated capability, maybe a year or two ahead of it, so that when the value does arrive you're not bottlenecked on hardware.

r001.rationale: The response discusses long infrastructure lead times and investment based on expectations, but does not mention TSMC or the absence of advance purchase commitments.

r002.rationale: It says building ahead can prevent hardware bottlenecks and falling behind, but does not state that doing so reduces the adjustment costs of an abrupt later expansion.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify early large AI training runs as a way to learn how to execute future infrastructure expansion.

astra-6.text:
I think some of that investment necessarily has to come ahead of the economic value. You need the chips, the data centers, and the power infrastructure in place before you can train and deploy the systems that produce that value. So I wouldn’t expect investment and revenue to move in lockstep.

But there’s a question of how far ahead you should build. If you’re investing on the expectation that AI will generate very large revenues several years from now, you’re taking a risk both on capabilities improving and on people finding useful ways to deploy those capabilities. A system being impressive doesn’t immediately translate into businesses being willing to spend a lot of money on it.

So I think the sensible approach is to anticipate demand, particularly for infrastructure with long lead times, while making further investment conditional on evidence that demand is actually materializing. You want to avoid infrastructure becoming the bottleneck, but you also don’t want to treat projected economic value as though it’s already been realized.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you need investment in chips and infrastructure to happen ahead of the economic value being realized, because that infrastructure is what enables you to train and deploy the systems that generate the value. You can’t wait until the demand is fully apparent and then instantly build the data centers and power supply to serve it. There are substantial lead times.

But that creates a difficult forecasting problem. Investors have to anticipate how capable these systems will become, how much people will pay to use them, and how quickly deployment will happen. If they’re too optimistic, you can end up with excess capacity and disappointing returns. If they’re too cautious, infrastructure becomes a bottleneck and delays the benefits.

So I wouldn’t expect investment and revenue to move in lockstep. Investment should lead, but the size of that lead should depend on the evidence about capabilities and demand. And I’d distinguish the social value of building that infrastructure from the returns to a particular investor: AI could produce substantial economic benefits without every company investing in it earning a good return.
